LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN) — Nigerian militants who sent a message to U.S. President George W. Bush saying they had struck two oil pipelines on Monday have called on former U.S. President Jimmy Carter and actor George Clooney to assist in resolving grievances in the oil-producing Niger Delta.

Military police were seen patrolling the waterways around the Omadino community in the Warri South area of the Niger Delta.

The group, known as the Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta, or MEND, said in its letter that it had targeted two pipelines it believed belonged to Chevron Corp. and Shell Oil. A representative for Royal Dutch Shell confirmed that one of its pipelines had been damaged the previous week. He said the incident would reduce exports by 169,000 barrels per day while crews worked to fix the pipeline. According to the spokesman, the pipeline is jointly owned by Shell along with Nigerian, French and Italian oil firms.

Chevron spokesman Kurt Glaubitz told CNN, however, that “No Chevron pipelines have been vandalized in Nigeria.” Nigerian authorities did not immediately respond with a statement.

In the letter, the militants described themselves as “commandos” and said their objective was “the crippling of the Nigerian oil export industry.”

The group said the attack was driven by what it called continuing injustice in Nigeria’s Niger Delta, where it claimed the underlying problems had not been dealt with by what it described as an illegitimate and dishonest government.

MEND also said it had previously sent two other letters to Bush and to actor George Clooney, and it requested that former President Jimmy Carter become involved. Clooney, a United Nations Messenger of Peace, has advocated for an end to the prolonged conflict in Darfur and for expanded humanitarian assistance there.

Carter was in the Middle East at the time, where he had met with exiled Hamas militant leader Khalid Meshaal as part of what Carter described as a “study mission” aimed at promoting peace, democracy and human rights in the region.

“MEND is prepared for talks and will prefer Ex President Jimmy Carter to mediate. Mr. Carter is not in denial as the rest of you who brand freedom fighters as terrorists,” the letter said. It added: “The ripple effect of this attack will touch your economy and people one way or the other and hope we now have your attention.”

The organization also claimed the pipeline strikes were a reaction to the arrest of one of its members, Henry Okah, who was detained the previous year and, according to local media accounts, faced treason charges.

Since late 2005, MEND fighters have launched repeated attacks against Nigeria’s oil industry and kidnapped many foreign workers, almost all of whom were later freed unharmed. The group has previously said it intensified its operations to protest what it views as an unfair sharing of Nigeria’s oil revenues.

In an unusual appeal, MEND called on former U.S. presidents George W. Bush and Jimmy Carter, as well as actor and activist George Clooney, to help draw attention to the grievances of people in the Niger Delta. The group has often argued that armed attacks on pipelines and other oil facilities are meant to pressure the Nigerian government and international oil companies to address local demands, including greater control over oil revenues, environmental cleanup, and development for affected communities.

The latest attacks damaged a pipeline connected to Shell operations, forcing a temporary reduction in shipments of about 169,000 barrels per day. Although production disruptions in Nigeria are not new, the scale of the cut underscored the vulnerability of the country’s oil infrastructure and the continuing instability in one of Africa’s most important energy-producing regions.

Nigeria is a major oil exporter, and unrest in the Niger Delta has repeatedly affected global supply calculations. While the Nigerian government has periodically launched security operations and offered amnesty programs to militants, the underlying issues of environmental damage, unemployment, corruption, and unequal distribution of oil revenue have remained sources of anger.

MEND’s claim of responsibility and its appeal to international figures show how the group seeks both military and symbolic leverage: damaging oil infrastructure to disrupt revenue while trying to attract global attention to the region’s complaints. ## Nigerian rebels claim Niger Delta pipeline attacks; Shell cuts shipments by 169,000 barrels a day

**LAGOS, Nigeria** — Nigerian militants said they carried out new attacks on oil pipelines in the Niger Delta, escalating pressure on the country’s petroleum industry and prompting Shell to cut crude shipments by **169,000 barrels per day**, according to company and militant statements.

The militant group, the **Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta**, or **MEND**, claimed responsibility for strikes on oil infrastructure in the southern delta region, where much of Nigeria’s crude is produced. The group has waged a campaign of sabotage, kidnappings and threats against international oil companies, saying it is fighting for greater local control of the region’s oil wealth and compensation for environmental damage.

Nigeria is one of Africa’s largest oil producers, and violence in the Niger Delta has repeatedly disrupted output, rattled international markets and heightened concerns about supply from the Gulf of Guinea.

### Shell confirms major shipment reduction

Shell said the attacks forced it to reduce shipments by **169,000 barrels per day**, a significant cut in production from the delta. The company did not immediately provide full details on the damage or how long the disruption might last.

Pipeline attacks in the Niger Delta often lead companies to shut down production as a precaution while they assess damage, secure facilities and conduct repairs. Such shutdowns can affect export schedules and trigger force majeure declarations if companies are unable to meet contractual delivery obligations.

Shell has long been a major operator in Nigeria, but it has also been one of the companies most affected by unrest in the delta, where militants have targeted flow stations, pipelines, export terminals and oil workers.

### Chevron denies militants’ claim

MEND also claimed to have attacked a pipeline linked to **Chevron**, but the company denied that its facilities had been hit.

Chevron said its operations were not affected by the alleged attack and rejected the militants’ account. The conflicting claims underscored the difficulty of verifying events in the maze of creeks, swamps and remote communities where oil infrastructure stretches across the Niger Delta.

Militant groups have sometimes exaggerated or misidentified targets, while oil companies often release limited details for security reasons.

### MEND seeks international attention

In an unusual attempt to draw global attention to its campaign, MEND said it had sent letters to **U.S. President George W. Bush** and actor **George Clooney**.

The group said the letters were intended to highlight conditions in the Niger Delta and raise awareness of what it describes as exploitation of local communities by the Nigerian government and foreign oil companies.

MEND has frequently used e-mails and public statements to communicate with journalists, governments and oil companies. Its messages typically combine political demands with threats of further attacks unless the Nigerian government releases detained leaders, redistributes oil revenue and addresses pollution and poverty in the delta.

### Oil wealth, poverty and militancy

The Niger Delta is the heart of Nigeria’s oil industry, but many communities in the region remain poor despite decades of crude production. Residents have long complained of oil spills, gas flaring, unemployment and the absence of basic services.

Militant groups have capitalized on those grievances, though Nigerian officials and analysts have also linked some armed factions to oil theft, ransom kidnappings and political violence.

MEND emerged as one of the most prominent militant organizations in the region, using attacks on pipelines and kidnappings of foreign oil workers to pressure both the government and multinational oil companies.

### Broader impact on Nigeria and oil markets

Repeated attacks in the delta have reduced Nigeria’s effective oil output at various points, complicating government revenue projections and contributing to volatility in global energy markets.

Nigeria relies heavily on oil exports for national income, and any sustained cut in production can affect government finances, foreign exchange earnings and investor confidence.

The latest disruption adds to the security challenges facing oil companies operating in the delta, where protecting pipelines is particularly difficult because infrastructure runs across vast, hard-to-monitor terrain.

### Government response

Nigerian authorities have in the past deployed military forces to protect oil installations and pursue militants, but crackdowns have sometimes deepened tensions with local communities. Negotiations, amnesty efforts and development promises have also been used at different times to reduce violence.

The latest attacks suggest that militant pressure on the oil sector remains a serious threat, especially when groups such as MEND can combine physical sabotage with international publicity campaigns aimed at amplifying their message.

For Shell, Chevron and other operators, the immediate concern is securing facilities and restoring production. For Nigeria, the larger challenge remains unresolved: how to stabilize the oil-producing delta while addressing the political, economic and environmental grievances that have fueled years of unrest.
